prompts.corals-kinds-signs:
Use case: AI-illustrated hobby guide that helps a beginner reef-aquarium keeper recognise what is wrong with their corals and anemones.
LOOK: every cell is a natural, clear, believable photo of a coral or anemone in an ORDINARY HOME REEF TANK: live rock with some pink coralline, white sand, a few other corals around, normal blue-white reef LED lighting. Clean water and clean glass: do NOT shoot through algae-covered, smudged or dirty glass, no heavy grime, no piles of detritus. The named coral is the clear subject: large in the frame, roughly centred and fully in view, NOT hidden behind rock, NOT cut off by the cell edge, NOT seen from an extreme angle, not an extreme macro. Not studio-perfect either: an everyday hobbyist photo with natural colours, an ordinary tank background and slightly uneven light. Show the problem the way it typically really looks on that coral in a home aquarium (the whole colony, how much of it is affected, how the polyps or tentacles look), NOT one tiny perfect mark on an otherwise perfect healthy coral. The problem must be easy to see at thumbnail size. Photographic and believable. Not cartoons, icons, illustrations, diagrams, 3D renders or typography. No people, hands, tools or equipment unless the cell names it. Absolutely no text, letters, numbers, labels, logos, watermarks, arrows or symbols anywhere in the image.
STRICT CONTACT SHEET for cropping into twelve separate pictures: exactly FOUR equal-width columns and THREE equal-height rows, twelve equal square cells covering the complete image edge to edge. No gutters, no borders, no outer margin. Every cell is its own separate tank photo with its own background. Nothing crosses a cell boundary; keep the main subject inside the central 85 percent of its cell. Never put a cell's subject into another cell. Follow the exact row-major order below.
Corals (draw each one exactly as named): ACROPORA = a branching small-polyp stony (SPS) coral, a bushy colony of finger-like branches covered in tiny polyps. MONTIPORA PLATE = a thin, flat, plating montipora (Montipora capricornis), orange or red, in overlapping plates. HAMMER CORAL = Euphyllia ancora, fleshy tentacles with hammer- or anchor-shaped tips on a branching skeleton. TORCH CORAL = Euphyllia glabrescens, long flowing tentacles with rounded coloured tips. BRAIN CORAL = a rounded, ridged LPS brain coral (lobophyllia or favia). ACAN = Acanthastrea, a colony of round, fleshy, colourful polyps. TOADSTOOL LEATHER = Sarcophyton, a mushroom-shaped cap on a thick stalk, covered in small polyps. MUSHROOM CORAL = Discosoma, flat round discs. ZOAS = zoanthids, a carpet of small button polyps with bright coloured centres on a rock. BUBBLE-TIP ANEMONE = Entacmaea quadricolor, a sea anemone whose tentacles have round bulb tips, its foot tucked into a rock crevice. AIPTASIA = small, brown, see-through pest anemones on thin stalks. Exactly the corals each cell names, at a believable home-aquarium size.
Row 1 column 1: HEALTHY SOFT CORALS: a fully open TOADSTOOL LEATHER coral with all its polyps out, a few green MUSHROOM CORALS and a bright patch of ZOAS on the rock beside it.
Row 1 column 2: HEALTHY LPS CORALS: a green HAMMER CORAL and an orange-tipped TORCH CORAL, both fully extended and puffy, side by side on the rock.
Row 1 column 3: HEALTHY SPS CORALS: a colourful branching ACROPORA colony with purple tips and a fuzzy look from its extended polyps, and an orange MONTIPORA PLATE below it.
Row 1 column 4: a HEALTHY BUBBLE-TIP ANEMONE, fully inflated, bulb-tipped tentacles spread wide, a pair of clownfish nestled in it.
Row 2 column 1: a BLEACHED ACROPORA: the whole colony has turned pale bone-white, but the flesh is still on it and the tiny polyps are still visible; healthy coloured corals around it for contrast.
Row 2 column 2: FLESH PEELING OFF AN ACROPORA: on a brown-green acropora colony, bare bright-white skeleton is spreading up several branches from the middle of the colony, with a clear, sharp line between the coloured living flesh and the bare white skeleton.
Row 2 column 3: BROWN JELLY ON A HAMMER CORAL: one head of a green HAMMER CORAL is covered in a brown, slimy, snot-like jelly mass, the flesh underneath dissolving, strands of brown slime drifting off; the other heads are pulled in.
Row 2 column 4: a TOADSTOOL LEATHER THAT WON'T OPEN: the cap is shrunk and slumped, every polyp pulled in so the surface looks smooth and bald, while the corals around it are open.
Row 3 column 1: CORALS TURNING BROWN: a reef corner where an ACROPORA, a MONTIPORA PLATE and a TOADSTOOL LEATHER have all gone a dull, flat chocolate brown instead of bright colours.
Row 3 column 2: RED BUGS ON AN ACROPORA: a clear view of a few acropora branches, polyps pulled in and colour faded, dotted with many TINY RED-ORANGE SPECKS the size of pinheads.
Row 3 column 3: ACROPORA-EATING FLATWORMS: a clear view of acropora branches with several small, flat, TAN-BROWN OVAL WORMS sitting on the flesh, nearly the same colour as the coral, and a couple of small bare bitten patches.
Row 3 column 4: MONTIPORA NUDIBRANCHS: an orange MONTIPORA PLATE with several small orange-white sea slugs on it, the same colour as the coral, a few small bare white patches and white egg spirals near the plate edge.

review.method: Every sheet opened and every crop checked for the right coral, the problem visible at thumbnail size, Jez's 05:11 style (ordinary home tank, clean glass, subject large and fully in view, not half-hidden, no grime, not studio), nothing crossing cell edges and no text; full-size strips of the borderline crops and a labelled contact image of all crops reviewed (workspace/.openclaw/tmp/fhl-corals/all-crops.jpg).
review.styleResult: All five sheets came back as clear, natural home-tank photos: coral centred and fully visible, rock with coralline, white sand, blue-white LED light, clean water and glass. No algae-covered glass, no half-hidden subjects, no text, no cell-edge crossings.
repairs: corals-repair (one 4x3 sheet) retook five clear failures with two takes each and two weak cells once: sign-lps-closed (first take: hammer coral fully open; used the hammer shrunk into its skeleton, cell 0), cond-zoa-pests (first take: no white pox bumps; used cell 2, closed zoas covered in white pustules), sign-soft-bites (first take: read as a sparse zoa rock; used cell 5, zoas with torn polyps and a leather with a bite out of its cap), sign-anemone-unclear (first take: anemone half hidden in a rock crevice; used cell 6, half-open droopy anemone in full view), cond-anemone-stress (first take: anemone stretched up a glass corner looked like a pipe; used cell 8, anemone crawling across the sand), sign-sps-brown-jelly (first take: thin brown streak; used cell 11, thick brown slime with strands over the lower branches).

Not used: torch-coral take of sign-lps-closed (cell 1, also fine), second zoa pox take (cell 3, also fine), zoa-only nibbled take (cell 4, weaker), second anemone-unclear take (cell 7), anemone on the back glass (cell 9, looked like a floating jellyfish), sign-sps-closed retake (cell 10, no clearer than the first take, so the first take stays).

weakCells.sign-sps-closed: an acropora with its polyps in looks smooth and a little dull; by nature it is a subtle difference from a healthy acropora at thumbnail size (the retake was no clearer).
weakCells.sign-red-bugs / cond-red-bugs: the red specks are readable but small, as they really are; clearer on the larger result hero than on the sign tile.
weakCells.sign-sps-bites: only a few crescent bites with white skeleton, not dramatic.
weakCells.sign-peeling: the bare white skeleton runs up the centre branches with a clear line; reads a little like a white branch at the smallest size.
weakCells.sign-anemone: the deflated anemone sits in its crevice in somewhat dim light; the shrunken stringy shape is still clear.
weakCells.sign-anemone-bites: ragged tentacles are on one side only.
weakCells.cond-flow-placement: the powerhead is at the left cell edge; the coral bent away from it is clear.
